chunks: And Ibn Fadhal narrated from one who informed him from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
"Zihar (verbal divorce) does not occur except upon a part similar to the place of actual divorce."

It was said to him: The beginning of what is in these hadiths is that the two hadiths, which are the last two, are mursal (disconnected) and not musnad (connected), and the ruling for this is that it is not objected against the musnad hadiths, even though the last hadith is general, and it is permissible for us to specify it with those hadiths, so we say that in Zihar, all that is observed in divorce is observed, such as the two witnesses, the woman being pure (from menses), and that he intends divorce, and other than that of the conditions, except if it is attached to a condition, for this ruling is specific to Zihar rather than divorce.

Even though his saying (peace be upon him) in the first report, 'There is nothing upon you,' can be understood as meaning 'There is no punishment upon you,' then he forbade him from repeating it to that extent, because uttering Zihar is prohibited, and mentioning it is not permissible, because Allah, the Exalted, said: 'And indeed they say a hateful speech and a lie. And indeed Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving.'

And it is also possible that he meant 'There is nothing upon you' before the condition occurs, although it becomes obligatory upon him after its occurrence, because we have proven that when Zihar is attached to a condition, the expiation is not obligatory in it except after the occurrence of the condition.
And that which adds clarification to that is what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for Zihar to be valid and how does it differ from standard divorce in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi examines the jurisprudential scope of Zihar, clarifying that its validity mirrors the conditions of Talaq (divorce) but remains distinct in its penalty structure, particularly for conditional declarations. The text resolves interpretive ambiguities regarding the Prophet's statement 'no penalty upon you' by distinguishing between the prohibition of the utterance itself and the timing of the expiation obligation. This analysis underscores the Shia scholarly method of reconciling apparent textual contradictions through precise legal categorization.
